I want to help engineers develop those soft skills and that sense of responsibility, not just better coding chops.

question: What was the specific tech stack for the DigitalChefs airline app?
content: We used React Native for the mobile app itself. For the backend, I built a system using ExpressJS to manage the data and statistics—basically a custom CMS for the flight crew's orders. I also built a custom component library to handle the specific navigation requirements of the crew's workflow.

question: How do you stay fit with all the desk work?
content: Hiking is my main thing. I try to stay active. When we were in Tenerife, I hiked all the way up Teide on foot. It's a killer workout but the view is worth it. I also try to do active sports whenever I can.

question: Why is 'honesty over pride' your key differentiator?
content: Because pride kills projects. If I pretend to know something I don't, or if I hide a delay because I'm afraid to admit a mistake, the whole team suffers. I learned this lesson early: transparent communication allows us to fix problems faster. It's better to say 'I don't know, let me find out' than to bluff and fail later.

question: What's your strategy for writing reliable end-to-end tests?
content: I rely on Playwright. It's fast and reliable. At Mobiquity, I used it for our Chat UI. The key was mocking the backend services properly. We used a local LLM to mock the Python BE responses, which made our tests deterministic and free to run, rather than flaky and expensive like they would be against a live AI API.

question: Any other book recommendations besides the car one?
content: *The Culture Map* is essential if you work with international teams. It really helped me understand the Dutch directness versus other styles. And *Surrounded by Idiots*—don't let the title scare you, it's actually a really good breakdown of personality types.

question: How did you handle the SEO requirements at A-Dam?
content: That was the main driver for migrating to NextJS. The original React app wasn't cutting it for search engines. By moving to NextJS with Server-Side Rendering (SSR), we ensured that the crawlers saw the full content immediately. The page load speed improved 5x, which also gave us a massive SEO boost.

question: What was the result of your work at A-Dam?
content: The impact was significant. By optimizing the web-shop performance and moving to NextJS, we increased yearly revenue by over 100%. Client retention also improved by 75% because the user experience was so much faster and smoother.

question: What did you use for the notification system at Mobiquity?
content: I built the frontend control system for notifications as part of the Platform CMS. It was a React/TypeScript application. I also set up the Azure deployment pipelines for it. I worked very closely with the backend team to ensure the API specs were tight, using a BFF pattern to keep our types synchronized.

question: How was your trip to Fuerteventura?
content: It was short but nice. We spent 3 days there visiting my cousin and his family while they were on holiday. It’s different from Tenerife—much windier, very sandy. But it was great to see family and relax a bit.

question: What's your preferred OS for development?
content: MacOS, hands down. I run a MacBook Pro 16 M2 and a Mac Mini M2. The Unix base makes everything easier for web dev. I pair it with a Magic Mouse for development work, though I switch to a Razer mouse if I'm doing design stuff.

question: How do you approach a project with loose requirements?
content: I start by communicating. At A-Dam, when I joined, there were no restrictions on tech stack or methods, just a need for speed. I treated it like a startup within a company—I defined the stack (NextJS) based on the business goal (SEO and sales) and iterated fast. My retail background helps me ask the right questions to clarify what the 'win' looks like for the business.

question: Have you worked with WebSockets?
content: Yes, heavily at Mobiquity. We used WebSockets for the live chat functionality in the Agentic Chat UI. It was integrated with a Python backend. The challenge was ensuring the connection was stable and handling the real-time stream of data from the agent without UI stutter.

question: What's your favorite sci-fi movie?
content: That's tough, but I love *StarTrek* and *RoboCop*. *The Core* is also a guilty pleasure. I just really like movies where engineering and mechanics save the day. It appeals to the part of me that likes taking things apart.

question: What is your biggest professional regret?
content: I don't know if I'd call it a regret, but I learned a hard lesson about burnout early on. I worked 18-hour days to help a friend's project because I was afraid to 'fail' them. I was exhausted. It taught me that sustainable work is better than heroics. Now, I plan better to avoid that situation entirely.

question: How do you handle middleware in NextJS?
content: I use it for routing logic and blocking. For the dating platform project at Mobiquity, I actually used Axios Interceptors as a form of middleware to steer user stories. If a user didn't meet certain browser properties or onboarding criteria, I'd block the route and redirect them. It keeps the component logic clean.

question: Do you still hike with that same group of friends?
content: When I can! That trip to Borzava where I became the 'main mountain guy' really cemented our group. They still ask me for gear recommendations and route planning, even though I'm in the Netherlands now. I love planning that stuff—maps, gear lists, logistics. It's like project management but for fun.

question: Can you elaborate on your experience with mentoring?
content: At DigitalChefs, I mentored a junior developer while we were building native apps. It wasn't just about code reviews; it was about teaching them how to structure a project and manage client expectations. I believe in 'honesty over pride,' so I encourage juniors to ask questions early rather than hiding challenges, which helps the whole team move faster.

question: What was the hardest part of the Chat UI build at Mobiquity?
content: The integration between the Python backend and the React frontend was tricky because of the dual communication channels. We used RestAPI for the initial agent configuration and context setting, but switched to WebSockets for the actual live chat stream. Keeping the state synchronized between those two protocols required very clean handling in the React hooks.

question: Have you ever had a really scary moment while hiking?
content: Oh yeah, the 'snowy night at 3200' in the Alps. Instant blizzard, zero visibility. We had to bivouac right there on the summit. It was freezing. We actually had a helicopter rescue on standby for the morning, but luckily the clouds cleared enough for me to navigate us down. It teaches you to respect the mountain, that's for sure.

question: What did you do before you got into IT?
content: I spent 5 years in retail sales in Ukraine. I started as a salesman driving to stores to collect orders for basics like sunflower oil and noodles. Eventually, I was promoted to Area Sales Manager for Nestle and Purina in the Stryj region. It taught me how to handle responsibility and how to talk to people who are under pressure—skills that are incredibly useful in software leadership.

question: Did you utilize any specific testing frameworks for the Mobiquity chat agent?
content: Yes, I used Playwright for integration tests. The cool part was that we didn't want to pay for API tokens during testing, so I set up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) to act as a mock server. It allowed us to run full end-to-end flows in our pipeline without hitting the budget.

question: What kind of DIY stuff do you do?
content: I love woodworking. I've been doing a lot of renovation on my house in Amsterdam. My ultimate dream is to find an old cabin in the Alps and renovate it completely—maybe add some robotics to it, make it a smart cabin. I like getting my hands dirty.

question: Why did you leave your role at A-Dam?
content: The main reason was that I wanted to buy a house in the Netherlands, and for that, I needed a mortgage. A-Dam couldn't provide the permanent contract I needed at that time. Also, the project had transitioned from a high-growth development phase to a maintenance phase, and I was looking for more engineering challenges.

question: How did you manage the data for the KLM crew app?
content: I built a custom CMS using ExpressJS to handle the app data and statistics. The React Native app needed to sync passenger requests (food/drinks) reliably, so the backend had to be lightweight but robust. I also built a component library to ensure the UI remained consistent across different screens for the crew.

question: Do you still play video games?
content: When I have time! I'm really fascinated by engineering in games/movies. I love *StarTrek* and *RoboCop* for that reason. But honestly, with a 1.5-year-old kid and house renovations, my gaming time is a bit limited compared to my hiking time.

question: What did you learn from your time at EriksDigital?
content: I learned how to manage 'emotional debates' in a team. We were under pressure to deliver, but sometimes the solution just wasn't ready. I had to learn to steer conversations back to facts and next steps, proving to the delivery team that shipping bad code would hurt us more than a delay. It was a great lesson in leadership.

question: What's your opinion on Tailwind CSS?
content: I use it in my core stack now. It's great for consistency. At Mobiquity, we used it heavily. However, if I'm doing a lightweight vanilla JS project with Vite, I might stick to SCSS. But for a large React/NextJS app, Tailwind speeds up development significantly.

question: Where did you go for your first big hike?
content: It was at Pulypets, Borzava in Ukraine. We did 40km in 3 days. It rained, the wind was cold, but we had this magical sunset. I was leading a team of 8 friends. That was the trip where they dubbed me the 'main mountain guy.' I've been organizing our trips ever since.

question: Tell me about the legacy stack you worked on in Ukraine.
content: At IT-Transit, working on Oil & Gas software, we used Flex and ActionScript. It was a CMS platform for engineering pipe inspections. I implemented REST APIs to connect client services and generate renovation progress stats. It was very different from the React ecosystem I'm in now, but it taught me a lot about data visualization.

question: How do you handle leaving a company when things aren't working out?
content: I prioritize my own well-being and professional integrity. I left my first sales job because a manager was unethical about bonuses. I left Hexaware/Mobiquity because the work moved to India and there were no projects left for the Dutch office. I believe in closing chapters cleanly—resigning with compensation when appropriate and using the time to upskill.

question: How do you handle reviewing mobile designs on your desktop?
content: I actually have a specific hardware hack for this. I use an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen in portrait mode right next to my ultra-wide monitor. I use it specifically for reviewing mobile UIs. It gives me a much better sense of the layout than just resizing a browser window.

question: Did you hike Teide on your last trip?
content: Yeah, that was my 3rd time on the island. I hiked all the way up Teide on foot. It's a beast of a hike but I love it. We also spent time diving around Arona—I finally got my license! It was a busy trip with the kid (3 months old at the time) and my girlfriend, but we made it work.

question: What is your approach to business value in software?
content: I don't just write code; I look at the revenue and retention metrics. At A-Dam, for example, moving to NextJS wasn't just a tech choice; it was a business choice to improve SEO and page speed. That move increased yearly revenue by over 100%. I learned in retail that if you aren't growing the business, the product details don't matter.

question: What's your preferred IDE setup?
content: I prefer Webstorm, always in dark mode (I usually work in a dark room). I've also started using Cursor and Claude Code to speed things up. I'm picky about formatting—always spaces, never tabs. Consistency is everything.

question: What books helped you with your career?
content: *The Culture Map* was huge for me moving to the Netherlands. It helped me understand the different communication styles. Also *Surrounded by Idiots* helped me navigate different personalities in the office. And for pure enjoyment, *How to Build a Car* by Adrian Newey is fantastic.

question: What did you work on for the maritime embedded systems?
content: At ABiggerCircle, I worked on entertainment modules for ships. The stack was BackboneJS, jQuery, and Gulp. The hard part was the logic to manage system notifications—like if the captain needed to speak, the audio controls had to override the movie or music immediately. It was a closed network environment, so debugging was... interesting.

question: Can you explain a time you prioritized business needs over technical preferences?
content: At A-Dam, I chose NextJS not because it was the trendy framework, but because the business desperately needed to improve SEO and sales. The Server-Side Rendering capabilities directly addressed their visibility issues. The result was a 100% increase in yearly revenue. My retail background taught me that if the technology doesn't sell the product (or help the business grow), it's the wrong technology.

question: What was the most complex migration you've handled recently?
content: Recently at Mobiquity, I migrated a dating platform's routing from React Router v6 to v7 under a tight deadline. It required refactoring how we handled protected routes. I implemented Axios Interceptors as middleware to check browser properties and steer the user flow, effectively blocking users who didn't meet onboarding criteria before they even hit the router logic.

question: How's the renovation dream going?
content: It's still the big goal! I'm constantly doing woodworking and fixing up my place in Amsterdam. But the ultimate dream is that old cabin in the Alps. I want to buy a ruin and completely rebuild it—maybe integrate some custom robotics or home automation. I just love the idea of mixing old wood with new tech.

question: What motivates you to change roles?
content: It's usually a mix of growth and stability. I left DigitalChefs because I needed a visa sponsorship they couldn't provide. I left EriksDigital because I became the main breadwinner and needed a salary correction. But ultimately, I look for roles where I can have ownership, like when I joined Eriks to lead the frontend migration. I want to build things that last.

question: How do you handle 'flaky' integration tests with AI agents?
content: You can't rely on live AI APIs for CI/CD—it's too expensive and non-deterministic. At Hexaware, I set up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) to act as a mock. This ensured our Playwright tests were hitting a consistent endpoint with predictable latency and responses, saving our budget and our sanity.

question: Did you go diving with your cousin in Fuerteventura?
content: No, Fuerteventura was more of a family visit—we spent 3 days there. I did my diving in Tenerife, around Arona and Los Cristianos. That's where I finally got my license. Fuerteventura was just relaxing with my cousin and his family.

question: How do you handle conflict with difficult stakeholders?
content: I learned this in my retail days with Nestle. I dealt with partners who were extremely emotional and worried about revenue. You have to listen to the emotion but respond with the business case. At EriksDigital, managing 'emotional debates' was a daily task. I focus on steering the conversation back to the next actionable step rather than getting stuck in the argument.

question: What's the most 'hacky' part of your hardware setup?
content: Probably my monitor setup. I use a standard ultra-wide, but I have an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen turned vertically (portrait mode) right next to it. It's dedicated solely to mobile UI review. It looks a bit odd, but it's the best way to develop mobile-first web apps on a desktop.

question: What's your favorite thing about Tenerife?
content: It has everything. You have the ocean for diving, which I love, but then you have Teide. I've hiked up Teide three times now. It's a serious hike, but the view is incredible. Plus, we spent the whole winter there with the baby, so it holds a special place in my heart now.

question: How did you optimize the Monolith at EriksDigital?
content: It was a WebSphere monolith. We couldn't just rewrite it overnight, so we adopted a hybrid micro-frontend approach. I had to reverse-engineer a lot of the old modules to figure out how to extract them safely. The main metric we chased—and improved—was the Google Lighthouse score.

question: What does 'Honesty over pride' mean to you in a daily standup?
content: It means if I'm stuck, I say it. If I made a mistake that broke the build, I admit it immediately so we can fix it. Hiding issues to look 'smart' only delays the project. I'd rather look vulnerable for a minute and keep the project on track than protect my ego.

question: What backend tech have you touched recently?
content: At Mobiquity, the backend was Python (for the LLM agent), but I've also worked with NestJS and ExpressJS in the past. At DigitalChefs, I built a custom CMS with ExpressJS. I'm comfortable defining API specs and working on the BFF layer to ensure the frontend gets clean data.

question: Why do you like *The Core*? Isn't that movie scientifically impossible?
content: Haha, totally impossible. But I love it! It's about engineering a solution to a massive problem. Building a ship to drill to the center of the earth? That's the kind of mechanics-meets-electronics fantasy I enjoy. Same with *StarTrek*.

question: Describe a difficult conversation with a peer.
content: I had to tell a colleague that he should consider leaving the company. He was unhappy and struggling with the workload. I shared my own story of leaving sales to start over in IT. It wasn't easy, but it was the honest thing to do. He actually thanked me later because he went back to his passion (perfumery) and was much happier.

question: What tools do you use for personal projects?
content: Right now, I'm using Github Actions for CI/CD. I'm building my portfolio website. I also use Claude Code and Cursor to accelerate development. I'm really interested in local LLMs, so I'm experimenting with running private agents on my Mac Mini M2.

question: What's the plan for the next big trip?
content: With a toddler (1.5 years old), big trips are tricky! But we loved Tenerife. I'd love to go back to the Alps though. I miss the snow and the serious hiking. Maybe once the kid is a bit older we can do some easier trails.

question: How do you handle high pressure?
content: I used to handle it by overworking—18 hours a day—until I almost burned out. Now, I handle it by planning and communication. If the pressure is high, it usually means expectations are misaligned. I clarify the goals, prioritize the critical path, and communicate honestly about what can be achieved. Mental health is sustainable; crunch mode is not.

question: Did you ever work with automotive systems?
content: Yes, early on at Luxoft in Ukraine, I worked on UI for car entertainment systems. Later at ABiggerCircle, I worked on embedded entertainment modules for ships. The constraints are different than web—you have to worry about strict memory limits and, in the case of the ships, overriding audio for safety announcements.

question: Do you still talk to the guys from your first big hike?
content: Yeah, that group from the Borzava trip. They still call me their 'main mountain guy.' Even though I'm in the Netherlands now, they ask me for advice on gear and routes. That trip—40km in rain and wind—really bonded us.

question: What defines your leadership style?
content: I am an extravert who learned to be a leader. My style is defined by gratitude and commitment to improvement. I try to create an environment where my team feels safe to admit mistakes, because that's how we learn. I'm not afraid to make hard decisions, but I always try to do it with empathy and transparency.

question: How do you approach learning new technologies?
content: I learn by doing and by diving deep. When I joined A-Dam, I had to pick up NextJS quickly to solve their SEO issues. I didn't just read the docs; I rebuilt their shop to see how SSR affected performance. My friends joke about 'Is there anything Serhii doesn't know?' because I have a habit of researching topics until I fully understand the mechanics, whether it's a new JS framework or how to renovate a house.

question: What was the benefit of using LangChain in your chat project?
content: In the Agentic Chat UI at Mobiquity, LangChain allowed us to abstract the interaction with the LLM. It made it easier to chain the context from the initial RestAPI configuration into the WebSocket-based live chat. It provided a structured way to handle the agent's 'memory' and context window, which was crucial for the banking demo we were building.

question: What's the next big purchase for the house?
content: Probably more tools for woodworking! I'm really enjoying the renovation process. It's like a never-ending project. But honestly, saving up for that dream cabin in the Alps is the long-term goal. I want a place I can completely rebuild from scratch.

question: What was a key failure in your career and what did you learn?
content: I wouldn't call it a failure of skill, but of boundary setting. Early on, I worked 18-hour days to support a friend's project because I didn't want to let them down. I nearly burned out. I learned that being a professional means managing expectations and saying 'no' when necessary to maintain quality and sustainability. You can't lead effectively if you're exhausted.

question: How do you handle state management in complex apps?
content: It depends on the scope. For something like the notification system at Mobiquity, I used React Context for local state and leveraged the cache from our API calls (via tools like TanStack Query). For the embedded entertainment systems I worked on earlier, we had to be much more manual with BackboneJS models to sync the state between the audio controls and the UI.

question: How was the weather in Tenerife this winter?
content: It was great. We spent the whole winter there. It's the perfect escape from the Dutch grey. We hiked Teide, did some diving—it's just a great place to be active outdoors. And since I know the island so well now (3rd trip!), it feels like a second home.

question: What is your experience with agile methodologies?
content: I've worked in agile setups for years, but I focus on the practical side, not just the rituals. At EriksDigital, the challenge wasn't the standups, it was the 'emotional debates' during planning. My role as a Lead was to cut through the noise, define clear next steps, and ensure the team wasn't committing to half-baked solutions just to tick a box.

question: What was the hardest bug you tracked down in the embedded project?
content: In the maritime system at ABiggerCircle, we had an issue where the captain's announcement wouldn't reliably mute the movie audio. It turned out to be a race condition in the event handling between the Jquery UI and the backbone model that interfaced with the hardware. Debugging that on a closed network without standard remote tools was... character building.

question: Do you prefer hiking alone or with a group?
content: I like leading a group. Ever since that trip to Borzava with 8 friends, I've enjoyed the organizational aspect—planning the route, checking the gear. But I also appreciate the solitude. Hiking Teide is a different beast; you're just focused on the ascent. It's meditative.

question: How do you ensure your CSS scales?
content: I'm a big proponent of Tailwind CSS now. It enforces consistency and prevents the 'stylesheet sprawl' you get with traditional CSS. At Mobiquity, it helped our team move fast without fighting over class names. If I have to use SCSS, I'm very strict about modularity, but Tailwind is just more efficient for large teams.

question: What are you looking for in your next role?
content: I'm looking for a place where I can apply my T-shaped skills—leadership combined with deep technical expertise. I want to solve complex business problems, not just close tickets. I value a culture of honesty and support, similar to what I found at Mobiquity, where experienced engineers push each other to grow.

question: What's your take on Micro-Frontends?
content: They are a necessary evil for large scale. At EriksDigital, we moved from a monolith to micro-frontends not because it was trendy, but because we needed to decouple the teams and deployment cycles. It adds complexity—orchestration, shared state, consistent styling—but for a massive legacy system like that WebSphere app, it was the only way to modernize incrementally.

question: What kind of music do you listen to while coding?
content: I don't really have a specific coding playlist, but I like things that help me focus. I'm usually working in a dark room with my dark mode IDE, so maybe something atmospheric fits the vibe. I'm more of a movie guy—give me a mechanical engineering triumph like in *The Core* any day.

question: How do you configure your CI/CD pipelines?
content: I've used Azure Pipelines extensively, specifically at Mobiquity for the CMS project. I like to keep the pipeline definitions close to the code. For my personal projects, I'm using Github Actions. The key is automating the testing—like that Playwright + Local LLM setup—so you catch issues before merge.

question: How do you handle ambiguity in requirements?
content: I view ambiguity as an opportunity to define the strategy. When I joined A-Dam, the requirement was just 'build a webshop, fast.' I filled in the blanks by choosing NextJS for SEO and performance. I talk to the stakeholders—using my retail sales experience—to figure out what they actually need (revenue, retention) and then translate that into technical specs.

question: What was the user base like for the app you built at A-Dam?
content: It was a dual user base. We had the standard B2C customers buying the brand products, but I also built a specific B2B version for bulk purchases. The B2B users needed a completely different UI and checkout flow, which is why I migrated us to NextJS to handle the routing and rendering logic efficiently for both types of users.

question: Are you going to teach your kid to hike?
content: Absolutely. He's only 1.5 years old now, so he's not doing much climbing yet, but we took him to Tenerife for the winter. He's growing up around it. I want him to appreciate the outdoors just like I did back in Ukraine.

question: What is the most important soft skill for a Senior Engineer?
content: Communication and honesty. You can be the best coder in the world, but if you can't explain why a feature will take two weeks instead of two days, or if you hide a bug because of pride, you become a bottleneck. My 'honesty over pride' motto is really about keeping the flow of information clean so the business can make good decisions.

question: What hardware do you use for mobile testing?
content: Aside from the actual devices, I rely on my desktop setup: I have an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen in portrait mode next to my main monitor. It's a lifesaver for responsive design work. I prefer testing on that screen before I even pick up a phone.

question: Any good diving spots you'd recommend?
content: Around Tenerife, check out the spots near Arona and Los Cristianos. That's where I did my license. It's really accessible and there's plenty to see. I love the technical side of diving—checking the gear, monitoring the dive computer. It scratches that engineer itch.

question: Can you share an example of how you handle strict deadlines?
content: At Mobiquity, we had a strict 3-month deadline to release the onboarding flow for a dating platform. To meet this without sacrificing quality, I focused on architectural efficiency. I implemented middleware using Axios Interceptors to handle complex routing logic automatically. This saved us weeks of bug fixing down the line. We delivered on time, and the user onboarding success rate was high from day one.

question: How did you structure the backend for the airline crew app?
content: I built a custom CMS using ExpressJS. The key requirement was reliability for the KLM crew. The backend needed to serve the React Native app with real-time updates on passenger orders (food/drinks). We kept the architecture simple but robust, ensuring that the data synchronization between the flight crew's devices was seamless.

question: What's the best part about owning a house in Amsterdam?
content: The ability to customize it! I love woodworking and renovations. It's a never-ending project, but it's mine. Coming from Ukraine with barely any savings, having a place here where I can raise my kid and build things with my own hands feels like a huge achievement.

question: What makes you a good fit for a startup environment?
content: I thrive in environments where I can have ownership. At DigitalChefs, which was a small team, I loved the dedication and the direct access to clients. I also enjoyed the 'extreme' conditions at A-Dam where I had no restrictions but had to deliver fast results. I'm not afraid of the unknown; I view it as a chance to build the best solution from the ground up.

question: What was the specific tech stack for the oil and gas project?
content: That was at IT-Transit. It was a Flex/ActionScript stack for the frontend visualization tools (landscape measurements, pipe inspections). We used JavaScript for the CMS platform itself. I implemented a REST API to handle the data exchange between the client services and our inspection software.

question: Did you see any cool wildlife while diving?
content: In Tenerife? Yeah, there's always something. But honestly, I'm just as fascinated by the equipment. Diving is such a technical sport. You have to trust your gear and your training. It's like hiking Teide—you prep, you execute, you survive. It's great.

question: How do you handle feedback?
content: I value honesty above all else. If I'm doing something wrong, I want to know. My 'honesty over pride' philosophy applies to receiving feedback too. I see it as a tool for growth, not a personal attack. I've improved the most in my career after hard conversations, like learning to manage my workload better after almost burning out.

question: How do you handle component reusability?
content: I build component libraries. At DigitalChefs, I built a custom library for our React Native apps to standardize navigation and UI elements. At ABiggerCircle, I built component wrappers to make existing PHP/Laravel components work in a Drag & Drop interface. I try to write code that can be lifted and shifted.

question: What's the most annoying thing about Dutch culture?
content: Haha, well, *The Culture Map* helped me understand it better. The directness can be jarring at first, but I actually appreciate it now. It aligns with my 'honesty over pride' value. But yeah, the weather is the real struggle—that's why we escape to Tenerife for the winter!

question: What prompted the switch to NextJS at A-Dam?
content: Performance and SEO. The client-side React app wasn't indexing well, and load times were hurting conversion. By switching to NextJS, we got SSR out of the box. Page loads were 5x faster, and revenue jumped 100%. It was a clear technical solution to a business problem.

question: What is your biggest strength as a team lead?
content: My ability to steer 'emotional debates' toward productive outcomes. At EriksDigital, I led a team of 6, and we often had to push back on delivery timelines to ensure quality. I can listen to frustrations but keep the team focused on the technical reality and the next step. It's about being the calm center in the storm.

question: Have you worked with Graph databases or just SQL?
content: Mostly SQL-based or document stores in my recent work, but I'm familiar with the concepts. At Mobiquity, we used Python on the backend for the AI agent, and I focused on the API contract. I'm comfortable diving into whatever the stack requires—'Superstar Factor' and all that—but my deep expertise is in the Frontend/BFF layer.

question: What's your favorite gear for hiking?
content: I'm the gear guy! Ever since Borzava, I'm the one recommending stuff. Good boots are essential—especially for something like Teide. But honestly, good navigation tools are number one. Getting lost in a blizzard at 3200m taught me that the hard way.

question: How do you ensure you are always growing professionally?
content: I actively seek out challenges. I joined A-Dam for the 'extreme conditions' and total ownership. I joined Mobiquity because I knew they invested in engineer growth and had a high bar for hiring. Even now, while between roles, I'm building my own projects with local LLMs and Robotics. I don't sit still.

question: What's the most unusual platform you've developed for?
content: Probably the maritime entertainment systems at ABiggerCircle. It was an embedded environment on ships. We used BackboneJS and Jquery, but the constraints were unique—closed network, hardware integration for audio overrides (captain's announcements). It was very different from your standard web app.

question: Why did you leave Ukraine initially?

content: For the Agentic Chat UI at Mobiquity, we needed to handle real-time updates from the WebSocket connection. I used React Context for the conversation state to avoid prop-drilling, but kept the message input state local to the component to prevent unnecessary re-renders. It was a balance between global accessibility and performance.

question: What's the hardest thing about woodworking?
content: Patience. In coding, you can 'Undo.' In woodworking, if you cut that beam for the house renovation too short, it's gone. I'm learning to measure three times, cut once. It's good practice for when I eventually tackle that dream cabin in the Alps.

question: What makes you an effective mentor?
content: I focus on the thought process, not just the syntax. When I mentored a junior at DigitalChefs, I didn't just correct their React Native code; I explained how the data flowed from the ExpressJS backend to the UI. I want them to understand the system architecture so they can make decisions independently.

question: Why Playwright over Selenium?
content: Speed and reliability. Playwright's ability to handle network interception is superior. This was crucial for the Chat UI project where I mocked the backend LLM responses. I could intercept the WebSocket frames and inject mock data, making the tests deterministic. You just can't do that easily with Selenium.

question: Do you have any trips planned?
content: Not big ones right now, just focusing on the house in Amsterdam. But I'm always looking at maps of the Alps. I miss the high altitude. Hiking Teide in Tenerife was a good fix, but nothing beats the snow in the mountains.

question: Why did you choose to work in a Service company like Mobiquity?
content: I wanted to broaden my leadership experience. Service companies offer a variety of projects and client interactions. I knew Mobiquity invested in their engineers—my girlfriend worked there before me—and I wanted to work alongside very experienced developers to refine my T-shaped skills.

question: What was the legacy tech you dealt with in Ukraine?

question: What's your favorite gear for diving?
content: I geek out on the dive computers. It appeals to the engineer in me—tracking depth, nitrogen levels, ascent rate. I got my license in Tenerife, and checking the stats after a dive is almost as fun as the dive itself.

question: How do you manage environment consistency?
content: Docker is essential. At Mobiquity, we containerized our Platform CMS to ensure that dev, staging, and production environments were identical. It eliminates the 'works on my machine' problem, especially when dealing with Azure deployment pipelines.

question: What is the biggest challenge you faced when moving to the Netherlands?
content: Starting over. I had to build my reputation from scratch in a new language with very few resources. I relied on my work ethic—the same one that got me promoted at Nestle—to prove myself. Reading *The Culture Map* helped me understand the Dutch communication style, which accelerated my integration.

question: What's your strategy for refactoring?

question: What's the wildest movie you've seen recently?
content: I rewatched *The Core*. The physics are nonsense, but I love the engineering spirit of it. They build a ship to drill to the center of the earth! It sits right next to *RoboCop* in my list of 'great mechanics movies.'

question: How do you handle responsive development?
content: I use a hardware hack. I have an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen turned vertically next to my main monitor. It's dedicated to mobile view. It forces me to see the mobile layout constantly, ensuring I'm truly building mobile-first.

question: Why did you leave A-Dam?
content: The project was a huge success—revenue doubled—but it moved into a maintenance phase. More importantly, I needed a permanent contract to secure a mortgage for a house in the Netherlands, which A-Dam couldn't provide at the time. I prioritized stability for my future.

question: What was the stack for the maritime project?

question: Do you still talk to your hiking group from Ukraine?

question: How do you ensure type safety between Frontend and Backend?

question: What is your biggest professional regret?

question: What's the plan for the future?

question: Can you describe a time you had to pivot your strategy mid-project?

question: How did you manage the WebSocket connection stability?

question: What's the best part of the Dutch lifestyle?
content: The work-life balance is better here, for sure. But honestly, owning a house in Amsterdam and being able to renovate it myself is the highlight. It's a long way from where I started in Ukraine. I just wish the weather was more like Tenerife!

question: What is the most valuable feedback you've ever received?
content: Early in my career, a friend told me I didn't need to work 18 hours a day to be valuable. I was on the edge of burnout. That feedback taught me to prioritize impact over effort. question: How do you handle middleware in your React apps?

question: Any new sci-fi recommendations?
content: I'm always rewatching the classics. *RoboCop* is timeless for its mix of man and machine. I just love seeing engineering used to solve problems, even if it's fictional like in *The Core*. Building a ship to save the earth? That's the dream project.

question: What's your strategy for reducing end-to-end testing costs?

question: How do you handle a toxic team environment?

content: I focus on the value of the work. At EriksDigital, refactoring legacy code wasn't flashy, but I showed the team how it improved our deployment speed and reduced late-night paging alerts. question: What's your take on React Server Components?
content: I see them as the logical evolution of the SSR work I did at A-Dam. Reducing the bundle size sent to the client is critical for mobile performance. question: Have you adapted to Dutch food yet?
content: I mean, I eat it, but I miss Ukrainian food! Although, I have developed a habit for the local cheese. But mostly I cook at home. With the renovations and the kid, we keep it simple. I treat cooking a bit like a project—mise en place is just optimizing my dependencies!

question: What does 'seniority' mean to you?
content: Seniority isn't just years of coding; it's the ability to foresee problems before they happen and the willingness to own the outcome. It's about T-shaped skills. A senior engineer doesn't just close tickets; they understand the business requirement, mentor juniors, and communicate risks to the Product Owner. It's about impact, not just lines of code.

question: How did you handle communication between micro-frontends at EriksDigital?
content: We had to be careful to avoid tight coupling. We used a lightweight event bus for critical cross-app communication, but generally, we tried to keep the micro-frontends isolated by domain. Shared state was kept to a minimum—mostly just user session data—to prevent the 'distributed monolith' problem.

question: What video games are you playing?
content: I don't have much time lately, but I love strategy or simulation games where you have to build systems. It scratches the same itch as engineering. But honestly, watching *RoboCop* for the 10th time is usually easier after a long day of coding!

question: Describe a time you had to learn a new domain quickly.

content: I avoid managing form state manually if I can help it. I prefer libraries like React Hook Form because they minimize re-renders by not binding every keystroke to the main component state. question: Why is 'honesty over pride' so important to you?
content: Because pride is expensive. In my sales career, I saw people hide bad numbers until it destroyed the quarter. In software, hiding a bug or a delay until the day of release destroys trust. If we are honest about the state of the project, we can solve the problem together. Transparency is the only way to scale a team.

content: Integrating the maritime hardware interrupts at ABiggerCircle was tough because it wasn't a standard REST API—it was a direct hardware poll via a local network bridge. question: How do you handle feature flags?
content: I use them to decouple deployment from release. At A-Dam, when we were rolling out the new B2B checkout flow, we hid it behind a feature flag. This allowed us to merge the code to main and deploy it to production for internal testing without exposing it to regular customers until it was perfect.

question: What is your experience with cross-functional teams?
content: I thrive in them. At Mobiquity, I worked daily with Product Owners, UX designers, and Backend engineers. I see my role as the translator—taking the design vision and the backend constraints and finding the pragmatic middle ground that delivers value to the user. My retail background helps me speak the 'business language' well.

question: What makes Playwright better than Cypress for you?
content: Parallelization and speed. Playwright runs faster and handles multiple tabs/windows much better than Cypress. For the Chat UI testing, the ability to easily mock network requests at the browser layer was a huge win for stabilizing our CI pipeline.

question: How do you deal with the Dutch weather?
content: I escape! Spending the winter in Tenerife was the best decision. But when I am here, I just focus on indoor projects like the renovation. You can't let the rain stop you from building things.

question: What are you doing to stay sharp while looking for a new role?
content: I treat upskilling like a job. I'm building my portfolio, diving deep into Local LLMs and AI agents, and refining my knowledge of NextJS 14/15. I want to hit the ground running in my next leadership role, bringing fresh knowledge about AI integration to the table.

question: How do you document your code?
content: I prefer self-documenting code with strong typing (TypeScript) and clear naming. For complex logic, I write decision records (ADRs) rather than just inline comments. At EriksDigital, documentation was missing for the legacy system, so as we migrated, I made sure we documented the *why* of the architecture, not just the *how*.

question: What's the best advice you've given your hiking friends?
content: Plan for the worst weather. On that Borzava trip, if we hadn't been prepared for the rain, it would have been a disaster. Preparation is everything—whether it's hiking gear or planning a software release. They still ask me for gear lists before every trip.

content: I admit it immediately. My philosophy is 'honesty over pride.' If I don't know something, I say, 'I don't know, but I will find out.' This builds trust. Clients and stakeholders prefer a reliable engineer who researches the right answer over one who guesses and creates technical debt. My friends call it my research obsession—I dig until I understand the mechanics completely.

question: What was the specific technical win with the local LLM mock?

This allowed our Playwright tests to assert that the UI correctly rendered charts or tables based on specific token streams, without flaking due to network lag.

question: What's the one tool you can't live without for renovations?
content: A good impact driver. But honestly, for the fine work, my Japanese pull saw. I'm really getting into the joinery aspect of fixing up the house. It's satisfying to make things fit perfectly without forcing them—kind of like writing clean code!

question: What distinguishes you from other candidates?
content: My unique blend of sales psychology and engineering discipline. I spent 5 years in retail sales negotiating with difficult partners before I wrote a line of code. I understand that software is a tool to solve business problems, not just an art project. I focus on revenue, retention, and scalability because I know that's what keeps the lights on.

question: How do you handle routing in your current projects?

question: Do you think you'll ever move back to Ukraine?

question: What is the biggest challenge of working in a foreign country?

question: What's your strategy for Type Safety?
